Ndamba

A coaching and match-analysis system built on a single game model, the Njangi Code, which links drill design, weekly load planning and live event tagging to a composite index of purposeful possession, from under-8 teams to the first team.

Visit the site ↗How to useEngineering record

Engineering recordFor technical reviewers

Designed and shipped a coaching app that works on a touchline without signal: offline match tagging, a computed performance index, a shared diagram format for app and books, and an assistant that prepares but never sends.

System architecture

  • React app, Wake Lock while tagging
  • Dexie: teams, sessions, matches, tags
sync

External services

During a match the coach taps events that are written to IndexedDB at once, with the screen kept awake. The Njangi Index and its five sub-indices are computed from those tags on the device. Mola, the assistant, runs a rules engine locally and calls Claude through a server function when available; every message, email or calendar file it prepares waits for the coach’s approval.

Key engineering decisions

01

Offline first for the touchline

Stadium networks fail; writing every tag locally first means a dropped signal never loses data.

02

One diagram format

A drill diagram is a JSON description rendered by both the app and the book tooling, so the printed and interactive versions never diverge.

03

Prepare, never send

The assistant drafts communications but a human sends them, which keeps an AI mistake from reaching parents or players.

Notes for reviewers

Limits and next stepsAdd cloud sync for multi-coach clubs and automated tests for the index computation; payments are not yet active.
01

Problem statement

Possession percentage says little about how a team actually plays. Many neighbourhood and academy coaches plan sessions on paper and recall matches rather than measure them, and clubs rarely keep the same game model and vocabulary from the under-8s to the first team.

02

Contribution

Ndamba puts one method into practice, possession with purpose, in which the ball circulates through the whole team like the pot of a njangi, a rotating savings group. Coaches retrieve its 64 drills with diagrams, assemble sessions and plan the week by days to the match, with training load charted. During a match a single tap from the touchline records each action; the tags are converted into the Njangi Index, five sub-indices, a written summary of how the team played and objectives for the following week. Video analysis, a player space with each player’s week, load and development, and Mola, an assistant that prepares work inside the application, complete the system. The coaching book and the first Lionceaux novel can be read in the app.

03

Architecture

React and TypeScript on Vercel. Team, session, match and tag data are stored in IndexedDB on the device, so tagging continues without a network while the screen is kept awake. Mola runs on a built-in rules engine and can call the Claude API through a server function. Lionceaux Football is a separate Unity WebGL build of about 25 MB, with a lighter version for phones.

04

Method and data

A single JSON description defines each pitch diagram, which therefore renders identically in the books and in the application. Every WhatsApp message, e-mail or calendar file prepared by Mola waits for the coach’s approval before it is sent.

05

Verification and limitations

The Njangi Index is a composite specific to this method rather than an industry-standard metric, and its reliability depends on consistent tagging. Mobile Money and card payments are not yet active; every plan can be tried in demonstration mode.
